title: The Mythical Man-Month
author: Frederick P. Brooks Jr.
theme: People and months are not interchangeable, so large software projects succeed through realistic scheduling, small coherent teams and a single unifying design, not through adding more hands.
summary: Fred Brooks wrote this collection of essays after managing the development of a large IBM operating system in the 1960s. His aim was to explain why big software projects so often run late and over budget, even when staffed by capable people. He compares them to a tar pit: no single problem traps the project, but many small ones together drag it down.

His central argument concerns the unit used to plan work. Counting effort in person-months assumes that people and time can be swapped freely, as they can in picking cotton. Software is different. Tasks depend on one another, and every new member must be trained and must communicate with the others, so coordination costs grow much faster than the team. This leads to his best-known rule: adding people to a late software project makes it later.

Brooks also warns that programmers are habitually optimistic and that schedules usually give far too little time to testing. He suggests that only a small share of the effort goes into writing code, while planning and testing take most of it.

For organising work, he proposes small teams built like a surgical team, with one chief programmer doing the core design and specialists supporting that person. Above all, he values conceptual integrity: a system should reflect one consistent set of design ideas, which usually means a small group of architects controls the design, separate from those who implement it.

Other essays describe the second-system effect, where designers overload their second project with every feature they held back from the first, and urge teams to plan to throw one version away, because the first attempt mainly teaches what should have been built. Brooks stresses written specifications and clear communication.
A later edition added his essay arguing that no single tool or technique will bring a tenfold gain in productivity, because the hard part of software is its essential complexity.
takeaway: When a project slips, protect design coherence and re-plan honestly instead of throwing more people at it.

questions.q: What is 'Brooks's law' as stated in the book?
options: Software costs double every two years
Every program contains at least one bug
Adding people to a late software project makes it later
Small teams always finish before large teams
questions.why: New members need training and add communication overhead, so they slow a late project further before they help.

questions.q: Why does Brooks call the man-month 'mythical'?
options: Because people and months are not interchangeable on tasks that require coordination
Because programmers rarely work a full month
Because software has no real cost
questions.why: The unit only works for tasks that can be split without communication, which software development is not.

questions.q: What large project shaped Brooks's views?
options: An IBM operating system developed in the 1960s
questions.why: Brooks managed IBM's OS/360 effort and drew his lessons from that experience.

questions.q: As a team grows, what happens to the effort spent on communication?
options: It grows much faster than the number of people
It shrinks as work is shared
questions.why: Each added person creates many new communication paths, so coordination costs rise sharply.

questions.q: Which activity does Brooks say schedules most often underestimate?
questions.why: He observes that testing takes a large share of total effort, yet plans usually leave little time for it.

questions.q: What does the 'surgical team' model propose?
options: One chief programmer does the core work, supported by specialists
Teams vote on every design choice
Medical staff are hired to manage projects
questions.why: Concentrating the core design in one skilled person, with others in support roles, keeps the work coherent and efficient.

questions.q: Which quality does Brooks consider most important in system design?
questions.why: A system that reflects one consistent set of ideas is easier to use and build than one assembled from many unrelated ideas.

options: Users prefer the second product they try
A second team is needed for maintenance
Designers overload their second system with features held back from the first
questions.why: Freed from earlier caution, designers tend to add every deferred idea, producing a bloated design.

questions.q: Why does Brooks advise teams to 'plan to throw one away'?
options: Because the first version mainly reveals what should have been built
questions.why: The first attempt is largely a learning exercise, so planning for its replacement avoids shipping a flawed design.

questions.q: What is the main claim of the 'No Silver Bullet' essay added in a later edition?
options: No single tool or method will bring an order-of-magnitude productivity gain
Large teams are the key to productivity
questions.why: Brooks argues that the hardest part of software is its essential complexity, which no single technique removes.
